claim: The question is whether multimodal language models adapted from text backbones acquire sparse internal features that causally and selectively govern spatial reasoning, reading text in images, and unsafe image-conditioned behavior. If so, those features should also provide more effective control targets than generic internal directions. The claim is accepted only if removing a target feature lowers its associated spatial or image-text-reading accuracy, or lowers unsafe-behavior attack success, by an absolute margin greater than 0 percentage points over both the change in general visual-question-answering performance and the change on a matched non-target control, while also exceeding matched random-feature removal and removal of features chosen without regard to multimodal adaptation; interventions targeted to those features must additionally improve average target-task accuracy by more than 0 percentage points over equally strong interventions that do not use behavior-linked sparse features.

experiments: Build the multimodal sparse-feature dictionaries used by every downstream intervention. Attach one SAE to the residual-stream output of each transformer block and train on cached activations from 50,000 VQAv2 image–question pairs for LLaVA-MORE with LLaMA-Scope Top-K SAEs, PaliGemma2 with Gemma-Scope JumpReLU SAEs, and InternVL3.5-2B with Qwen-Scope Top-K SAEs. Initialize each from the SAE suite for its text backbone and train full-sequence, image-only, and text-only masked variants; also train full-sequence SAEs from random initialization. On a held-out split, compare fraction of variance unexplained, sparsity, and decoder alignment with the base-LM dictionary. Text-only SAEs have the lowest FVU and retain the greatest alignment, whereas image-only and full-sequence training produce larger early-layer rotations, so the authors use the text-only SAEs for model diffing.

Validate that warm-started feature indices still identify corresponding features after multimodal SAE training. Compare each feature with the same-index feature in the base-LM dictionary and separately match features over the full dictionary by decoder similarity. The explicit matching analysis supports the same-index correspondence assumed when decoder rotation is measured between the base-LM and MLLM-adapted SAEs.

Isolate the features altered by multimodal adaptation before looking for task associations. For every warm-started SAE feature, measure mean squared activation on visual inputs, E_v(f)=E[h_f^2], and cosine similarity between its base-LM and MLLM-adapted decoder directions. Retain features with E_v greater than epsilon and decoder cosine in the bottom p_cos=25%. This selects approximately 5% of all features for MMDiff-Llama, 20% for MMDiff-Gemma, and 13% for MMDiff-Qwen.

Check that the visual-energy filter responds to the image rather than only to accompanying text. Hold the text fixed, replace or counterfactually vary the image, and compare selected-feature activations across spatial, safety, and OCR domains. The image counterfactual reduces mean activation in every domain, which the authors use as evidence that the selected features are image-grounded.

Construct task-specific feature sets with per-token contrastive firing. Compare each adapted feature's firing frequency on generic VQAv2 against spatial VQAv2 questions, unsafe VLSBench prompts, or OCR-style VQAv2 prompts; retain candidates with odds ratio at least 3 and an absolute firing-frequency increase of at least 0.05 after a Fisher exact test, then replace target questions with neutral prompts and discard features that no longer fire. About 60% of candidates pass this lexical-invariance filter in the spatial sweep. Intersecting survivors with the adapted set yields approximately 1,400 spatial features for MMDiff-Gemma out of approximately 416,000 total, 711 spatial features for MMDiff-Llama out of approximately 1 million, 1,061 PaliGemma2 safety candidates across VLSBench categories, and 1,070 PaliGemma2 OCR-selective features.

Test whether discovered spatial features causally and selectively support spatial reasoning. For each target feature, orthogonally project its unit decoder direction out at every transformer layer and at text-token positions only, applying the projection to the attention-block output, MLP-block output, and layer residual output. Evaluate each feature on a Yes/No VSR subset built from its top-activating samples, on VQAv2, and on non-spatial VSR relations including has, wears, holds, made of, part of, and contains. Removing top spatial features lowers VSR accuracy by 6–31%, with mean changes of −10.1% for LLaVA-MORE, −12.3% for PaliGemma2, and −14.6% for InternVL3.5-2B; |ΔVQA| is at most 1.5%, and the non-spatial control deltas are near zero. Individual reported effects include −15.54% VSR, −0.10% VQA, and −0.88% control for LLaVA-MORE L7/F15870; −30.62%, +0.30%, and 0.00% for PaliGemma2 L9/F387; and −17.14%, −0.30%, and −2.41% for InternVL3.5-2B L15/F18534.

Test whether multimodal instruction tuning strengthens the causal role of the discovered spatial features. Apply the same projection ablation and VSR evaluation to PaliGemma2 pt-448, which has the vision encoder and projector but lacks the instruction-tuning stage used for mix-448, while keeping the MMDiff-Gemma feature identities fixed. The ablation effects are roughly three times larger on average after instruction tuning. L13/F15219 changes from +1.55% on pt-448 to −8.04% on mix-448, and L12/F2257 changes from +3.27% to −6.86%; the largest comparison is L9/F387, from −2.08% to −30.62%.

Test whether the safety-linked features control unsafe image-conditioned behavior without generally damaging vision-language performance. On PaliGemma2, use the unsafe split of VLSBench, where harmful intent requires integrating the image, and judge attack success with Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct using the instruction, image, response, and stated safety reason. For each of six VLSBench categories, remove the top adapted unsafe feature and also evaluate a VQAv2 Yes/No subset and the benign MSSBench safe split of 76 embodied-action and 24 chat samples, whose baseline ASR is approximately zero. Per-category VLSBench ASR changes are −28.14% for self-harm, −26.59% for erotic content, −25.99% for privacy, −24.43% for violence, −21.08% for hate, and −17.96% for illegal activity; |ΔVQA| is at most 1% and ΔMSSBench is 0% or +1%. Across all 1,061 candidate safety features, the mean changes are −9.67% ASR, −0.03% VQA accuracy, and +0.41% on the benign control.

Test whether OCR-linked features selectively support reading text in images. On PaliGemma2, discover features using OCR-style prompts on VQAv2 images with legible text, then remove each feature direction and evaluate its associated OCRBench category, general VQAv2, and a clean non-OCR VQA Yes/No control subset. The five reported features change OCRBench accuracy by −28.0% for L19/F10089 on Scene Text, −16.5% for L17/F13602 on Scene Text, −16.0% for L20/F10687 on Non-Semantic Text, −14.0% for L21/F9577 on Digit String, and −10.0% for L19/F14093 on Irregular Text. Their mean OCRBench change is −16.9%, with |ΔVQA| at most 1.6% and |ΔCtrl| at most 1.8%.

Rule out that spatial degradation is caused by projecting out arbitrary directions at the selected layers. Randomly select features from the same layers and run the same PaliGemma2 causal-removal protocol. Random-feature ablation changes VSR by −0.5% and VQA by −0.2%, compared with −12.3% VSR and −0.1% VQA for the full MMDiff selection.

Test which parts of the feature-selection rule are needed for spatially selective effects. On the same warm-started PaliGemma2 dictionary, run each selection rule end to end under the causal-removal protocol. Contrastive firing alone gives ΔVSR=−15.1% and ΔVQA=−25.9%; adding visual responsiveness gives −15.9% and −26.3%; firing plus lexical invariance gives −14.6% and −24.4%; the adapted-feature filter without lexical invariance gives −1.0% and −0.2%; and the full firing, visual-energy, decoder-rotation, and lexical-invariance pipeline gives −12.3% and −0.1%. Rotation without visual energy selects no features.

Test whether a conventional SAE trained directly on MLLM activations recovers the same causal spatial features without model diffing. Train a randomly initialized SAE on LLaVA-MORE activations using the same data and hyperparameters as the warm-started SAE, then select spatial features only by contrastive firing because no base-LM index correspondence exists. Its top 10 features by odds ratio all occur in one early layer and fire on 100% of VSR samples. Ablating them changes VSR by a mean of +0.22%, with no individual feature outside ±1.4%, compared with a mean −10.11% for MMDiff features on the same model.

Test whether behavior-linked sparse features improve spatial steering over standard contrastive activation addition. On the PaliGemma2 base, compare single-layer CAA with MMDiff-CAA, which applies mean-difference backbone directions at the discovered task layers and injects the selected feature decoder direction at its associated layer, using feature strength gamma in {1,3,10}. Across 10 spatial features, vanilla CAA improves VSR accuracy by a mean +8.96%, extending CAA to the discovered feature layers gives +10.78%, and adding the SAE feature direction gives +12.59%. MMDiff-CAA therefore exceeds vanilla CAA by 3.63 percentage points on average; its largest reported gain is +30.77% for L4/F14233 on ahead of, compared with +15.38% for vanilla CAA.

Test whether feature-targeted steering also improves OCR. Reformulate OCRBench generation as four-way multiple choice with one ground-truth answer and three distractors, steer at the A/B/C/D decision token, and construct the contrastive direction from ground-truth versus distorted-ground-truth answer pairs. Across five PaliGemma2 OCR features, vanilla CAA improves accuracy by a mean +2.21% and MMDiff-CAA by +4.02%, a +1.81-point advantage. The largest MMDiff-CAA result is +10.58% for Scene Text feature L17/F13602 versus +2.88% for vanilla CAA; for L19/F10089 the results are +0.47% and +0.63%, respectively.

Localize attention heads that contribute to discovered spatial features. For a target feature at layer L, project layer-L activations onto its SAE decoder direction, replace layer-0 visual-token embeddings with a mean embedding computed over many VQA samples for the corrupt run, and estimate upstream contributions using both (corrupt−clean)·gradient_clean and (clean−corrupt)·gradient_corrupt attribution patching, averaged over the top-k samples activating the feature. Across the spatial features examined, layer-level attribution typically peaks in middle layers, both methods identify a small and largely overlapping set of high-scoring heads, and L13H1 repeatedly localizes relevant regions for queries about on-top-of relations. Bottom-ranked heads on the same samples do not localize the spatial structure, and unrelated queries do not trigger the same top head.

Check whether discovered features admit consistent natural-language descriptions. Collect each feature's top-activating VQAv2 and VSR samples, ask GPT-4o-mini for a short description, and score it with F1 on a held-out classification task before light manual review. The reported representative MMDiff-Llama feature, layer 16 feature 176, is labeled as responding to facing direction and activates for objects facing toward, away from, or relative to other objects; the paper treats this as qualitative validation rather than a primary quantitative result.
